newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta weakness seen curbing rate cut in Spain.
newsitem.headline: Peseta weakness seen curbing rate cut in Spain.

text.p: Worries over European monetary union and dollar volatility are curbing expectations of official Spanish rate cuts -- at least for now, economists said on Wednesday.
But although these same factors have brought the peseta to a one-year low versus the mark, they are unlikely to weaken it much further.

"The Bank of Spain wants a stable exchange rate.. this volatility is reducing the possibility the Bank of Spain might immediatly cut rates, despite benign inflation" said Felix Gonzalez, head economist at Beta Capital in Madrid.
The Bank of Spain has sharply cut its key money market rate in the last months. It is now standing at six percent, three full points lower than it was at the beginning of 1996.
The last cut, 25 basis points, was on January 16 at the first official repo after the peseta had broken the key 84 level. The peseta was trading around 83.50 per mark.
In January, supported by positive expectations over European economic and monetary union (EMU) convergence, the markets were discounting further cuts in the official money rate.
Some were anticipating it would end 1997 at around 4.5 percent.

"We have always said the market exaggerated these expectations. Still there is room to cut the official rate, although the peseta's weakness could delay a move," said Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
Short-term rates in the money market have reacted briskly to the new outlook for exchange rates, dealers said.
After many previous record lows, one-year Treasury bill yields rose to 5.172 on February 5 from 5.050 two-weeks before and to 5.315 percent today.

Since December 1995 the peseta has only blipped above 85 per mark a couple of times -- as on March 4, the day after a general election and at the end of July, right after the government had announced a surprise budget shortfall.
The peseta broke that level again on February 5, when London's Financial Times reported a plan to delay Italian and Spanish entrance in EMU.
"I do not think the peseta will go above 85 per mark," said Alzola adding, "we saw unwinding of previous foreign investor positions which should now be nearing an end."
The peseta was trading at around 1245 GMT at around 84.76/78 per mark, after hitting 84.85 earlier when dealers reported buying by the central bank.
The Bank of Spain, reported to have bought pesetas on several occasions in the past week, seems determined to maintain its unit relatively strong versus the mark.

"I think the peseta is curbed from falling much beyond 85 (to the mark) because the Bank of Spain has very ample reserves and has shown quite considerable determination in intervening slightly below that level" Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid told RFTV.
In January 1997 Bank of Spain currency reserves rose to $65,290.6 million from $39,439.7 million in January 1997.
Economists added around 84.50/85.00 per mark is the right level for the peseta, given its purchasing parity.
And as long as the peseta recovers its stability, the Bank of Spain could start cutting rates again.
"I still think the Bank of Spain will cut drastically its rate during this year. It's a matter of timing," said Bank of America's Lumnholdt.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
